title: February Product Updates: Less Paperwork, More Progress
summary: February Product Updates: Less Paperwork, More Progress
body_text: This month’s updates to the Recidiviz Corrections Platform, driven by insights and feedback from our partner agencies. Feature suggestions? Email feedback@recidiviz.org Better Meetings with Meeting Mode Automated Meeting Documentation: A new tool for supervision and facilities staff that records officer-client meetings and automatically generates structured outputs—draft case notes organized by topic (e.g., employment, housing, family), action items assigned to both the officer and the client with deadlines, status updates across key life domains, and full meeting minutes. Officers can focus on the conversation, not their notes. In-Meeting Notepad: During a recording, staff can jot down quick notes in a built-in notepad without leaving the tool—so nothing gets lost in the moment. Flexible Deployment: Meeting Mode works across supervision and facilities settings, and is accessible from any web browser—no special hardware or software required. Staff can print or export outputs for easy filing. Improved Audio & Transcript Tools for Case Planning Interactive Audio Player: A redesigned waveform-based audio player lets staff click on any point in the waveform to jump to the matching turn in the transcript—and vice versa. This makes it significantly faster to review recorded interviews and verify AI-generated summaries. Playback Speed & Download: Staff can now play recordings at 1x, 1.5x, or 2x speed, and download audio files in MP3 format for offline review or record-keeping. Speaker Assignment: For recorded interviews, transcripts now display all detected speakers with the ability to manually label who is who (e.g., "Client" and "Case Manager"), giving staff control over transcript accuracy. Search by ID: Staff can search for clients by DOC ID in addition to name, making it faster to pull up the right record—especially in states where staff are more familiar with ID numbers. Staff Review Tools: Case managers can assign assessments to individuals on their caseload, track completion, and review results, ensuring the full picture is available when it's time to build a case plan Calculating Accurate Release Dates Automated Time Comp: A new calculator encodes state sentencing statutes–including good time credits, violent offense floors, parole eligibility tiers, and prior custody credits–to automatically generate projected maximum and probable release dates and parole eligibility dates. This gives time comp staff a high-speed starting block to spend less time on manual math and more time on verification. Full Transparency: Every calculation is fully visible and traceable back to the underlying statute, so staff can audit the logic and build confidence in the outputs. The tool handles flexible unit aggregation (years, months, days) and accounts for standard vs. work/education good time rates. ‍ Redesigned Sentence Timeline: An updated sentence timeline gives staff a clearer, more interactive view of key milestone dates—from parole eligibility to max release—with improved styling and the ability to drill into individual dates for more detail. New Features for Residents Risk-Needs Assessments: Residents can now complete risk-needs assessments directly on their tablet, at their own pace and in their own words—freeing up staff time while giving individuals more agency in the case planning process. Browse Available Programs: Residents can explore a comprehensive, facility-specific catalog of available programs—from educational courses to vocational training—directly on their tablet. Each listing includes a description, eligibility requirements, and how much earned time the program offers. Save Programs of Interest: Residents can bookmark programs they're interested in, making it easier to plan their path and have informed conversations with their case manager.

title: Noble Corporation plc to announce fourth quarter and full year 2025 results
summary: HOUSTON, Feb. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Noble Corporation plc ("Noble" or the "Company") (NYSE: NE) today announces plans to report financial results for the
body_text: HOUSTON, Feb. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Noble Corporation plc (“Noble” or the “Company”) (NYSE: NE) today announces plans to report financial results for the fourth quarter and full year 2025 on Wednesday, February 11, 2026 after the U.S. market close. The Company’s earnings press release and accompanying earnings presentation will be available on the Noble website at www.noblecorp.com. Noble will host a conference call related to its fourth quarter and full year 2025 results on Thursday, February 12, 2026 at 8:00 a.m. U.S. Central Time. Interested parties may dial (800) 715-9871 and refer to conference ID 31391 approximately 15 minutes prior to the scheduled start time. Alternatively, participants may register for the conference call ahead of time at https://registrations.events/direct/Q4I313911. A live webcast link will be available on the Investor Relations section of the Company’s website, and a webcast replay will be accessible for a limited time following the scheduled call. About Noble Corporation Noble is a leading offshore drilling contractor for the oil and gas industry. The Company owns and operates one of the most modern, versatile, and technically advanced fleets in the offshore drilling industry. Noble and its predecessors have been engaged in the contract drilling of oil and gas wells since 1921. Noble performs, through its subsidiaries, contract drilling services with a fleet of offshore drilling units focused largely on ultra-deepwater and high specification jackup drilling opportunities in both established and emerging regions worldwide. For further information visit www.noblecorp.com or email investors@noblecorp.com. body_text: Aprender inglés sigue siendo una de las habilidades más importantes para crecer profesionalmente, comunicarse con el mundo y abrir nuevas oportunidades. Si estás buscando mejorar tu nivel de inglés este 2025, aquí te mostramos tres de los cursos más reconocidos en Chile , con distintos enfoques según tus objetivos, estilo de aprendizaje y disponibilidad. ‍ Los 3 mejores cursos de Inglés en Chile ‍ Poliglota: aprender inglés conversando desde el primer día Si tu meta es hablar inglés con confianza , Poliglota es una de las opciones mejor valoradas del país. Su metodología está basada en la práctica oral desde el primer día, en grupos pequeños guiados por coaches expertos. Es un curso 100% online, pero en vivo, con enfoque en conversación real y situaciones cotidianas. Los estudiantes destacan que no se aprende solo viendo o leyendo , sino participando activamente en sesiones donde se refuerza vocabulario, fluidez y seguridad al hablar. Además, hay acompañamiento personalizado, acceso a un plan adaptado a tu nivel y una comunidad activa de aprendizaje. Ideal si: Quieres perder el miedo a hablar Buscas resultados reales en pocos meses Necesitas flexibilidad y contacto humano real 👉 Haz tu test de nivel gratuito y recibe un plan personalizado. ‍ Open English: buena flexibilidad Open English es una plataforma conocida en toda Latinoamérica. Ofrece acceso ilimitado a clases grupales online y una amplia biblioteca de ejercicios interactivos, disponibles 24/7. Es una buena opción si valoras la flexibilidad total y prefieres avanzar a tu ritmo. Sin embargo, muchas clases se comparten con usuarios de distintos niveles y la práctica real de conversación puede ser limitada , especialmente si necesitas feedback directo o guía constante. Ideal si: Tienes horarios muy variables ‍ Ya tienes bases y solo quieres reforzar ‍ Te acomoda un modelo autodirigido ‍ British Council: estructura académica tradicional El British Council es un organismo reconocido a nivel mundial. En Chile, sus cursos online están diseñados para entregar una formación sólida en inglés general y preparación para certificaciones como el IELTS. Es una opción confiable si buscas un enfoque estructurado y tradicional , con materiales bien elaborados y estándares académicos altos. Eso sí, su metodología es más formal y no necesariamente está centrada en conversación fluida desde el inicio. Ideal si: Buscas certificar tu inglés Quieres una experiencia educativa formal Prefieres contenido académico ‍ ‍ ¿Aún con dudas? Revisa el comparador Si quieres comparar estas y otras opciones de forma más neutral, puedes visitar mejorcursoingles.com , donde encontrarás una comparativa externa de los principales cursos de inglés en Chile , con opiniones reales, ventajas y desventajas de cada uno. ‍ Conclusión No hay una única respuesta para todos. Pero si estás buscando una opción con interacción real, metodología práctica, clases en vivo y resultados visibles en poco tiempo, Poliglota destaca como una de las mejores alternativas para este 2025 . 👉 Empieza aquí con tu test de nivel gratuito ‍ ‍ ¿Por qué deberías tomar un curso de inglés ‍ Seguramente más de alguna vez te ha pasado que te toca enfrentarte al inglés , ya sea porque te tocó leer algo para tu trabajo, tus estudios o porque tuviste que darle indicaciones a un turista en la calle. ¿Te sentiste confiado a la hora de superar este obstáculo? ¿Notaste ciertas limitaciones? En estos y muchos otros casos tener un manejo adecuado del idioma puede abrirte muchas puertas tanto a nivel profesional como personal, sobre todo si estás buscando ascender en tu carrera o hacer un viaje por el mundo. Y si has estado pensando en hacer un curso de inglés de forma presencial u online, aquí te compartimos 3 motivos para comenzar hoy : ‍ 1. Es el idioma universal 🌎 ‍ Cuando estás en otro país sin hablar la lengua nativa y te toca comunicarte con un lugareño que tampoco conoce tu idioma, por lo general se recurre al inglés como lengua común. Esto debido a que en gran parte del mundo el inglés se enseña en las escuelas de manera obligatoria al ser una lengua predominante en el comercio internacional. Así que la razón número uno por la que deberías estudiarlo es porque te abrirá las puertas para comunicarte en gran parte del mundo. ‍ 2. Es más fácil de aprender que el español 🧐 ‍ Si bien aprender idiomas siempre tiene un grado de complejidad , muchos plantean que aprender inglés es más fácil que aprender español. Y si bien esta idea es debatible, lo cierto es que los verbos en inglés tienen una menor cantidad de conjugaciones que el español y los adjetivos no diferencian entre femenino y masculino. No obstante, muchos afirman que la gran complejidad del inglés radica en su fonética , es decir en cómo se pronuncian las palabras. Por eso, cuando te animes a estudiar inglés, es importante que practiques constantemente la pronunciación. ‍ 3. Te ayuda a crecer laboralmente 💼 ‍ Al ser considerado una lengua universal , el inglés puede encontrarse en todos lados, desde documentos con los que debas trabajar hasta las tiendas del centro comercial poseen palabras en este idioma. Por esa misma razón, muchas empresas hoy en día buscan profesionales con un alto manejo del inglés que logren comunicarse con proveedores internacionales o que puedan viajar sin problemas a otros países. Te compartimos algunas razones para estudiar inglés en Chile si aún no logras convencerte de estudiar este útil idioma. ‍ ‍ ¿Qué esperas para empezar a aprender? Dscubre por ti mismo/a cómo funciona el mejor curso de inglés en Chile .

title: Step-by-Step Guide to the Permitting Process
summary: Learn how the construction permitting process works step by step, from application to inspections and approval.
body_text: Key takeaways The permitting process typically includes research, application prep, submission, review, corrections, issuance, inspections, and final approval. Permitting requirements vary widely by city, county, and project type. The building permit inspection process is just as important as the initial application. Managing submissions with permit management software can shorten approval timelines and reduce manual work. ‍ If you build, renovate, install, expand, demolish, or alter a structure, odds are you’ll deal with the permitting process at some point. For some projects, pulling a building permit is relatively straightforward. For others, it involves multiple departments, plan reviews, corrections, inspections, and shifting local requirements. Either way, understanding the permitting process is key to keeping your project on track scaling your business. This guide breaks down the permit process for construction step by step so you know what to expect and how to move faster. Pull permits faster with PermitFlow. Learn how. ‍ Types of construction permits Not every project undergoes the same permitting process. Depending on scope, you may need one or several permits — and certain projects don't even require you to pull a permit Common examples include: ‍ Building permits Building permits are typically required for new construction, additions, structural changes, remodels, and major alterations. ‍ Trade permits Trade permits are required for electrical, plumbing, HVAC, mechanical, gas, fire protection, and similar systems. Many jurisdictions issue these separately from the main building permit. ‍ Demolition permits Demolition permits are required when removing all or part of a structure. This can apply to full teardowns, interior gut work, detached structures, and selective removals, depending on the municipality’s demolition permit. ‍ Zoning or land use approvals Some projects need zoning clearance before a building permit can be issued. Use, setbacks, lot coverage, height limits, parking, and occupancy can all come into play. 👉 Read more on zoning permits vs building permits . ‍ Specialty permits Depending on jurisdiction, this can include right-of-way permits, signage permits, grading permits, environmental approvals, historic review, solar permits, and more. 👉 For a broader breakdown, see our guide to types of construction permits . ‍ The typical permitting process At the end of the day, location is the biggest factor in how you’ll navigate the permitting process. Every city, county, and state (the authority having jurisdiction, or “AHJ”) handles permitting a little differently. That said, most projects move through the same core stages. Understanding how to pull a permit can help you plan better and avoid delays. ‍ Step 1: Identify the jurisdiction and reviewing agencies Many projects require more than one approval source. Depending on the property location and scope, your project may involve: City building department County permitting office Planning and zoning department Fire marshal Public works / engineering Health department Utility providers Historic preservation board Environmental or stormwater agencies HOA or architectural review boards (private, but often timeline-critical) This is especially common for commercial developments, subdivisions, multifamily communities, restaurants, medical spaces, and industrial work. You might think you only need a building permit, then later discover: Zoning approval is required first Civil plans need engineering signoff Fire suppression needs separate review Utility release is needed before final approval Understanding the approval path early is one of the best ways to reduce delays. ‍ Step 2: Confirm whether you need a permit The first step is to determine whether the work you’re planning actually even requires a permit. You might be surprised what does and what doesn’t require a permit. In most jurisdictions, permits are commonly required for: New buildings and additions Structural changes Kitchen and bathroom remodels Roofing replacements Window and door replacements (in many jurisdictions) Electrical service upgrades Rewires and panel changes HVAC replacements or new systems Plumbing repipes or sewer work Decks, patios, and accessory structures Demolition work Tenant improvements and change of use projects Some minor cosmetic work — like painting, flooring, cabinetry replacement without plumbing or electrical changes, or finish updates — may not require permits. The same may be true regarding like-for-like replacements. The only reliable answer comes from the local authority having jurisdiction (AHJ). Requirements vary widely, even between neighboring municipalities. ‍ Step 3: Define the project scope clearly Permit reviewers need to understand exactly what is being built or changed. A vague description of the scope of your work creates confusion and will probably end up triggering requests for clarification or corrections. Weak scope: Interior remodel Strong scope: Interior tenant improvement including non-structural partition changes, new lighting, two restroom fixture replacements, HVAC duct revisions, and finish upgrades. Accuracy matters here. It’ll help you pinpoint: Correct permit type Applicable codes Required plan reviewers Fee calculations Inspection milestones Whether licensed trades are needed This matters for trades too. A “furnace swap” may still require duct changes, gas line work, electrical disconnect updates, and combustion air compliance. ‍ ‍ Step 4: Prepare plans, drawings, and supporting documents Preparing your project plans is one of the most important parts of the construction submittal process. Regardless of your location, the AHJ isn’t going to want enough documentation to confirm your proposed work is up to code and matches site conditions. Commonly required residential or trade project documents: Contractor license information Scope of work Manufacturer spec sheets Load calculations Site sketch Energy compliance forms Homeowner authorization Commonly required commercial project documents: Architectural plan sets Structural drawings MEP plans Accessibility details Fire/life safety sheets Civil/site plans Engineering calculations Product approvals Existing vs proposed layouts Occupancy/use details Inaccurate or missing project plans and drawings are one of the most common reasons submissions get delayed. Getting this documentation right the first time can mean the difference between getting your permit on the first try and navigating five rounds of back-and-forth. ‍ Step 5: Submit the application correctly Once your documents are ready, it’s time to formally submit your permit application. Submission methods vary by jurisdiction. You might be asked to submit via: Online permitting portal Email In-person counter Hybrid system (e.g., upload online and pay in person) Accuracy matters more than many applicants realize. Simple mistakes can send your application back before it’s even thoroughly reviewed. On the application, you’ll probably need to provide: Property address Parcel/APN number Owner information Contractor information License numbers Job valuation Detailed scope Occupancy type Square footage Uploaded plans and attachments For companies pulling permits at scale, standardizing this step saves a lot of time. ‍ Step 6: Intake review and acceptance Before the department begins its technical review, it might perform a completeness or intake check. In other words, they may verify that your application contains the minimum required items and is ready to enter the review queue. This intake review might include checking that: Required forms are attached Payment has been received Plans were uploaded properly Correct permit type was chosen Contractor credentials are active Required signatures are included If anything is missing, the permit may be marked incomplete, rejected, or placed on hold. This is a common hidden source of delay because many applicants think “submitted” means “in review.” Quite often, that’s not the case. ‍ Step 7: Plan review After the building department has confirmed that your application is complete, it enters technical review. At this stage, reviewers check whether your proposed work complies with applicable codes, ordinances, and safety requirements. Reviewers are looking for: Safe structural design Means of egress Fire separation and alarms ADA/accessibility compliance Proper equipment sizing Ventilation and energy compliance Site drainage and utility impacts Setbacks, lot coverage, use restrictions Plan review timelines vary wildly across jurisdictions. Some departments (especially those in large cities or rapidly growing counties) have substantial delays and wait times, while others can get your application reviewed in a matter of days. Here’s a broad overview of average plan review timelines: Simple over-the-counter trade permits : Same day to several days Standard residential remodels : 1–4 weeks Larger custom homes : Several weeks Commercial TI or new construction : Weeks to months Complex multi-agency development : Several months Backlogs, staffing levels, and project quality all affect timing. ‍ Step 8: Corrections, comments, and resubmittals Unfortunately, a lot of permits don’t pass first review – especially large or complex projects. Reviewers will issue correction notices requesting revisions or clarification if they notice something inaccurate or incomplete. Examples of requests for revisions you might receive: Add beam sizing Clarify exit signage Provide restroom accessibility dimensions Update energy forms Show smoke detector locations Provide roof attachment details Correct occupancy classification Add equipment cut sheets How you handle review comments can have a huge impact on the total permit timeline. Quite often, projects lose the most time after comments are issued, when revisions sit internally, responsibilities are unclear, or only part of the requested changes are addressed. ‍ Best practices for resubmittals Review comments immediately As soon as you get comments back, read the full correction letter or markups the same day if possible. Separate minor administrative items from design or engineering changes so the team knows what can be fixed quickly and what requires more substantial coordination. Assign each item to the right owner Every comment should have a clear responsible party. That may be the architect , structural engineer, MEP consultant, contractor, permit coordinator, or owner representative. If no one owns each item, comments tend to stall. Prioritize high-impact items first Some comments are simple drafting edits. Others affect layout, structural design, accessibility, or equipment selection. Tackle the items that could create cascading changes first. Coordinate architect, engineer, and trade input quickly Many corrections touch multiple parties. For example, moving rooftop equipment may affect structural loads, electrical routing, screening requirements, and mechanical plans. Quick coordination prevents conflicting revisions. Respond directly to every comment Provide a written response letter or matrix that addresses each reviewer comment one by one. State what changed, where it changed, and sheet references when applicable. This helps reviewers move faster on the second pass. Re-submit a complete package Don’t send partial updates unless the jurisdiction specifically allows it. Include all revised sheets, updated forms, response letters, calculations, and attachments together. Incomplete resubmittals could trigger another rejection or hold. ‍ Step 9: Permit issuance Once all reviews are approved and fees are paid, you’ll receive your permit. You may receive: Permit card Approved stamped plans Inspection record card Conditions of approval Posted jobsite documents Expiration dates and renewal rules At this point, work can usually begin legally, subject to conditions. But remember: permit issuance does not mean you are done with the process. ‍ Step 10: Building permit inspections The building permit inspection process ensures the work installed in the field matches the approved plans and complies with local codes. Permit approval gets a project started, but inspections are what move it through each construction phase. Most jurisdictions require inspections at specific milestones before work can continue or be concealed. For example, framing usually needs to be approved before you can install insulation and drywall, and underground utilities are typically inspected before trenches get backfilled. Inspection procedures vary by location. Some departments offer online scheduling portals and next-day appointments, while others may require several days of lead time. Common inspections: Foundation/footing: Conducted before or during concrete placement, depending on the jurisdiction. Inspectors may review excavation depth, rebar placement, anchor bolts, setbacks, and soil conditions Underground plumbing/electrical: Required before trenches are covered. Inspectors typically verify pipe materials, slopes, cleanouts, conduit placement, and burial depths Slab or under-slab inspections: Common when plumbing, vapor barriers, reinforcing steel, or embedded systems are installed before a slab pour Framing: Performed after structural framing is complete. Inspectors may review framing members, connectors, shear walls, hold-downs, stair geometry, headers, and structural details Rough electrical/plumbing/mechanical: Completed after systems are installed but before walls are closed. This may include wiring, ductwork, vents, piping, equipment connections, and clearances Insulation/energy compliance: Required in many jurisdictions to verify insulation values, air sealing measures, duct sealing, and other energy code items Drywall/lath/fire-resistance assemblies: Some jurisdictions require inspection of wall assemblies, shear nailing patterns, or lath before finishes are applied Fire protection systems: Separate inspections are often required for sprinklers, alarms, kitchen hood suppression, standpipes, or related life-safety systems Final inspection: Conducted when the project is substantially complete and ready for occupancy, turnover, or signoff. Inspectors verify life-safety items, finish conditions, equipment operation, handrails, address numbers, and overall code compliance ‍ Step 11: Final approval and closeout After the project has passed all required inspections, your permit can be finalized. Depending on project type, final closeout may include: Final permit card Certificate of Occupancy (CO) Certificate of Completion Utility release Trade final signoff Closeout documentation Closeout is crucial because open permits can create problems later during property sales, refinancing, insurance renewals, and tenant turnover. ‍ What can cause a permit to be denied? Permit denials, rejections, or holds are more common than you might expect. In some cases, the issue is technical. In others, it comes down to incomplete paperwork, conflicting information, or local zoning restrictions. That said, most permit problems are preventable if you prepare and submit your application carefully. Incomplete applications Missing forms, unsigned documents, or incomplete contact information can stop an application before plan review even begins. Incorrect permit type selected Applying for the wrong permit category can create delays or outright rejection. For example, a structural remodel submitted as a simple interior alteration may need to be reclassified and refiled. Missing or inadequate plans If your drawings don’t provide enough detail for reviewers to evaluate the work, expect to be hit with requests for revision or a flat-out denial. Common issues include missing dimensions, unclear scope, no structural details, or inconsistent sheet sets. Code compliance issues Plans that don’t meet current building, electrical, plumbing, mechanical, fire, or energy codes will be denied until revised. Zoning conflicts Even if the construction itself is sound, the project may not meet zoning requirements. Setbacks, height limits, parking minimums, lot coverage, occupancy use, signage rules, and historic district restrictions can all prevent approval. Contractor licensing or registration issues Some jurisdictions require active local registration, state licensing, insurance certificates, or trade-specific credentials before issuing permits. If those records are expired or missing, the permit may be placed on hold. Unpaid fees or outstanding balances Permit fees, impact fees, utility fees, or prior unpaid balances tied to the property may need to be resolved before your submission can be approved. Existing violations or open permits If the property has unresolved code violations, stop-work orders, or older permits that were never closed out, the jurisdiction may delay new approvals until those issues are addressed. Inconsistent project information If the scope described on the application does not match the plans, valuation, contractor listed, or other submitted documents, reviewers may reject the package until everything aligns. ‍ Keep projects moving with less friction. Let PermitFlow handle the research, submissions, and approvals. Learn more. ‍ Common challenges with the permitting process ‍ Every jurisdiction operates differently Permitting is highly localized. Two neighboring cities could have different application forms, submission portals, review timelines, inspection procedures, fee schedules, and code interpretations. What works well in one market may cause delays in another. If your company works across multiple municipalities, that inconsistency can be an operational headache. ‍ Unclear requirements upfront So many permitting delays begin before the application is even submitted. Some jurisdictions clearly publish requirements online, while others have outdated checklists, limited guidance, or project-specific requirements that only surface later. This leads to missing documents, wrong permit types, or incomplete plan sets. ‍ Slow plan review timelines Permitting delays are a contractor’s greatest – and perhaps most common – enemy. Between staffing shortages, seasonal surges, and significant backlogs, so many building departments take weeks or even months to review permit submissions. Even a flawless application can end up waiting in line longer than expected, which makes scheduling labor, materials, and customer commitments more difficult. ‍ Poor visibility into status So many contractors and builders still rely on email chains, spreadsheets, voicemail updates, or multiple portals to track permit progress. That creates common questions like: Has the permit been accepted? Is it in review? Who owes the next action? Were comments issued? Has the inspection been scheduled? Without centralized visibility, teams waste time chasing updates instead of moving work forward. ‍ Inspection scheduling bottlenecks Getting the permit is only part of the process. You also have to navigate inspections. Missed inspection windows, limited appointment availability, failed inspections, or unready job sites can stall projects after work has already started. ‍ Multi-jurisdiction growth complexity As you expand into new markets, permitting becomes harder to manage at scale. Each new city adds new contacts, new processes, and new local rules. What worked for five municipalities may break at 25. ‍ Changing codes and local policies Building codes, energy standards, zoning rules, and submission processes change regularly. A workflow that worked last year may be outdated today. Teams that don’t stay up-to-date risk avoidable corrections and delays. ‍ Tips for navigating the permitting process with ease The permitting process can feel unpredictable, but so many delays are avoidable. Moving permits faster isn’t a matter of luck – it means you’re more prepared, more organized, and more proactive from the start. These practical strategies can help whether you manage one project or hundreds: ‍ Tip 1: Start permitting earlier than you think One of the most common mistakes is treating permitting as something that starts after design is finished or after a project is sold. In reality, permitting should begin during the beginning stages of preconstruction . Early research into jurisdiction requirements, zoning constraints, lead times, and submission standards helps teams build more realistic schedules and avoid last-minute surprises. ‍ Tip 2: Confirm the correct permit path upfront Not every project follows the same route. Some scopes need only a trade permit. Others may require zoning approval first, multiple departmental reviews, or separate permits for fire, utilities, signage, or civil work. Clarifying the approval path early can prevent expensive rework later. ‍ Tip 3: Submit complete, coordinated packages Strong first submissions save time. Before filing, confirm that the application, plans, valuation, contractor information, and supporting documents all match. Incomplete or conflicting packages are one of the fastest ways to create delays. ‍ Tip 4: Write clear project scopes Vague descriptions invite questions. Instead of “remodel,” explain what is actually changing. Use specific verbiage, like structural work, new equipment, plumbing relocation, electrical upgrades, occupancy changes, or finish-only updates. ‍ Tip 5: Stay organized during review Once submitted, track every milestone: Submission date Intake acceptance Reviewer comments Resubmittal deadlines Fees due Permit issuance Inspection milestones Final signoff Permits often slow down because no one notices the next action item in time. ‍ Tip 6: Respond to corrections quickly and completely Reviewer comments are a normal part of the process. What matters is how quickly and thoroughly your team responds. Assign ownership immediately, coordinate revisions fast, and address every comment in one complete resubmittal whenever possible. ‍ Tip 7: Build local knowledge Every jurisdiction has its own preferences, workflows, and unwritten rules. Understanding those local nuances can make a major difference in approval speed. That knowledge may come from internal experience, trusted partners, or dedicated permitting support. ‍ Tip 8: Use systems that scale Spreadsheets, inbox threads, and scattered status updates may work for a small number of projects. But once your permit volume grows, it can become nearly impossible to keep track of everything. Permit management software like PermitFlow helps contractors, builders, developers, and architects centralize the entire process in one place. You can track permit statuses, assign ownership, manage deadlines, coordinate inspections, and maintain visibility across every active project. Instead of chasing updates across emails and spreadsheets, your growing team can use standardized workflows and real-time reporting to stay in control across multiple markets. ‍ FAQs How long does it take to get a building permit? Timelines vary widely based on jurisdiction, project scope, and workload. A simple trade permit may be approved in a few days, while residential remodels can take several weeks. Large commercial, multifamily, or multi-agency projects may take months. ‍ Who is responsible for pulling permits? That depends on the project and contract structure. It may be the general contractor, trade contractor , homeowner, developer , or owner’s representative. However, responsibility should always be clearly defined before work begins. ‍ Do I need separate permits for electrical, plumbing, or HVAC work? Often yes. Many jurisdictions issue separate trade permits even when there is an existing building permit for the overall project. This is common on remodels, additions, and commercial tenant improvements. ‍ Can I start construction before the permit is issued? In most cases, no. Starting work before approval can lead to stop-work orders, fines, failed inspections, and rework. It can also create insurance or contract issues if something goes wrong during unpermitted work. ‍ What if my permit expires before the project is finished? Some permits expire if work does not begin within a certain timeframe or if progress stops for too long. Depending on the jurisdiction, you may be able to request an extension or renew the permit, but you might have to reapply. ‍ Can a permit be transferred to a new contractor? Sometimes, but not always. Some jurisdictions allow contractor changes through a formal amendment process, while others require a new permit application or updated licensing documentation. ‍ What happens if permit plans change after approval? If the scope changes after issuance, revised plans may need to be submitted for approval. Significant structural, layout, occupancy, or system changes often require formal revisions before work continues. ‍ What happens if an inspector finds unpermitted work after? If an inspector discovers work that was completed without the required permit, the jurisdiction may issue a correction notice, stop-work order, or require a retroactive permit application. In some cases, finished work may need to be opened so hidden electrical, plumbing, or structural elements can be inspected. title: Honeywell and Vertiv to Improve Sustainability for Data Center Operations Across the Globe
summary: Data centers help enable the online applications that people depend on for work, entertainment and communications, but they require significant power to move information around the world. Today, two industry leaders announced a collaboration to create more sustainable and efficient data center operations.
body_text: Joint effort combines Honeywell operational technology experience with Vertiv’s critical digital infrastructure solutions to create more sustainable and efficient data center operations First joint offering to combine intelligent selection of energy resources with centralized visibility of operations and infrastructure to help reduce energy use ATLANTA AND COLUMBUS, OHIO [October 14, 2020] – Data centers help enable the online applications that people depend on for work, entertainment and communications, but they require significant power to move information around the world. Today, two industry leaders announced a collaboration to create more sustainable and efficient data center operations. Honeywell ( NYSE: HON ), a global leader in connected buildings, and Vertiv ( NYSE: VRT ), a global provider of critical digital infrastructure and continuity solutions, will work together to create integrated solutions to optimize data center sustainability, resiliency and operational performance. These solutions are expected to be available in 2020. The partnership builds on Honeywell’s industry-leading building management systems (BMS), operational software, and safety and security products along with Vertiv’s uninterruptible power supply (UPS), power distribution, thermal management, infrastructure monitoring and modular solutions to enable operators of hyperscale, large enterprise, co-location and edge data centers to integrate multiple domains of data within a data center. The companies will leverage building-operations data to drive optimization of operations, reducing energy use and costs while improving data center performance and sustainability. “Data centers face similar challenges as other buildings that have disparate systems that were not designed to work together, but they experience these challenges on a greater scale,” said Vimal Kapur, president and CEO, Honeywell Building Technologies. “We look forward to collaborating with Vertiv to offer integrated solutions that make it easier for data center operators to distill the mountains of data they pull from their equipment into actions that create more efficient and environmentally friendly operations.” “Business continuity is more critical than ever, with more people working, learning and connecting remotely, driving a simultaneous explosion in data and demand for new data centers. There is need and opportunity for data centers to be more efficient, reliable and sustainable,” said Rob Johnson, CEO, Vertiv. “Our collaboration with Honeywell will help us to collectively better serve our data center customers. Our offerings complement each other to provide greater value to data center operators.” Collaboration Improves Power Management for Uptime, Efficiency and Sustainability Data centers in 2018 consumed approximately 1% of the world’s energy use. i, ii While the industry has made great strides to reduce and offset energy demands, including increasing the utilization of renewable energy, more work can be done toward a more sustainable and carbon-neutral future. The companies’ initial focus will be on micro-grid solutions for data centers to enable more efficient integration of alternative energy sources such as solar arrays, fuel cells and batteries, and to provide a scalable approach for operators to quickly enhance functionality and improve total cost of ownership. The first offering from the collaboration will be an intelligent power management solution that features an energy resource management and supervisory control system in a single, integrated platform. Combining energy storage, analytics, forecasting and economic optimization, the solution will provide data centers with intelligent and autonomous selection of energy sources and grid services to operate a data center load and reduce energy costs while maintaining uptime requirements. The solution can help data centers meet availability requirements while optimizing energy costs, meeting corporate sustainability goals and reducing overall carbon footprint. It will also allow operators to better manage sustainability targets and account for external risk factors such as weather and grid reliability. Resilient Operations Backed by Trusted Brands The large amount of power used for thermal management, building systems and physical security within a data center can increase risk for downtime. The new scalable and easy-to-implement intelligent power management solution from Honeywell and Vertiv is designed to enable remote monitoring and maintenance, reduce costs, eliminate redundancy and improve power usage effectiveness (PUE). Combined, the companies sell industry-leading product brands that provide best-in-class differentiated support to data centers, including Honeywell’s advanced detection business featuring the VESDA brand of advanced smoke detection technology; Honeywell Forge enterprise performance management platform including Honeywell Forge Energy Optimization; Enterprise Buildings Integrator (EBI) and the Niagara Framework; and the Vertiv™ Liebert® power and thermal management solutions, Vertiv™ Avocent ™ monitoring and IT management solutions, and Vertiv™ Geist ™ power distribution solutions. To learn more about Honeywell and Vertiv data center collaborations, visit https://hwll.co/vqtw6 or http://b.link/3c94d . About Vertiv Vertiv brings together hardware, software, analytics and ongoing services to ensure its customers’ vital applications run continuously, perform optimally and grow with their business needs. As Architects of Continuity™, Vertiv solves the most important challenges facing today’s data centers, communication networks and commercial and industrial facilities with a portfolio of power, cooling and IT infrastructure solutions and services that extends from the cloud to the edge of the network. Headquartered in Columbus, Ohio, Vertiv employs approximately 20,000 people and does business in more than 130 countries. For more information, and for the latest news and content from Vertiv, visit Vertiv.com . About Honeywell Building Technologies Honeywell Building Technologies (HBT) is a global business with more than 20,000 employees. HBT creates products, software and technologies found in more than 10 million buildings worldwide. Commercial building owners and occupants use our technologies to ensure their facilities are safe, energy efficient, sustainable and productive. For more news and information on Honeywell Building Technologies, visit http://www.honeywell.com/newsroom . Honeywell ( www.honeywell.com ) is a Fortune 100 technology company that delivers industry specific solutions that include aerospace products and services; control technologies for buildings and industry; and performance materials globally. Our technologies help aircraft, buildings, manufacturing plants, supply chains, and workers become more connected to make our world smarter, safer, and more sustainable. title: Monster Beverage Declares Two-for-One Stock Split
summary: The Investor Relations website contains information about Monster Energy Company's business for stockholders, potential investors, and financial analysts.
body_text: Monster Beverage Declares Two-for-One Stock Split CORONA, Calif., July 08, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Monster Beverage Corporation (NASDAQ: MNST) today announced that its Board of Directors has approved and declared a 2-for-1 split of its common stock that will be effected in the form of a 100% stock dividend. Each stockholder of record on July 24, 2026 will receive a dividend of one additional share of common stock for each then-held share, to be distributed after close of trading on August 10, 2026. The Company anticipates its common stock to begin trading at the split-adjusted price on August 11, 2026. Monster Beverage Corporation Based in Corona, California, Monster Beverage Corporation is a holding company and conducts no operating business except through its consolidated subsidiaries. The Company’s subsidiaries develop and market energy drinks, including Monster Energy® drinks, Monster Energy Ultra® energy drinks, Juice Monster® and Punch Monster® Energy + Juice energy drinks, Java Monster® and Monster Killer Brew® non-carbonated coffee + energy drinks, Rehab® Monster® non-carbonated energy drinks, Monster Energy® Nitro energy drinks, Reign Total Body Fuel® high performance energy drinks, Reign Storm® and Storm™ total wellness energy drinks, NOS® energy drinks, Full Throttle® energy drinks, Bang Energy® drinks, FLRT™ total wellness energy drinks, BPM® energy drinks, BU® energy drinks, Burn® energy drinks, Live+® energy drinks, Mother® energy drinks, Nalu® energy drinks, Play® and Power Play® (stylized) energy drinks, Relentless® energy drinks, Samurai® energy drinks, Ultra Energy® drinks, Predator® energy drinks and Fury® energy drinks. The Company’s subsidiaries also develop and market craft beers, flavored malt beverages and hard seltzers under a number of brands, including Jai Alai® IPA, Dale’s Pale Ale®, Dallas Blonde®, Wild Basin® hard seltzers, The Beast™, Beast® Tea, Blind Lemon® and Blinder Lemon™. For more information visit www.monsterbevcorp.com . Caution Concerning Forward-Looking Statements Certain statements made in this announcement may constitute “forward-looking statements” within the meaning of the U.S. federal securities laws, as amended, regarding the expectations of management with respect to our future operating results and other future events including revenues and profitability. The Company cautions that these statements are based on management’s current knowledge and expectations and are subject to certain risks and uncertainties, many of which are outside of the control of the Company, that could cause actual results and events to differ materially from the statements made herein. Such risks and uncertainties include, but are not limited to, the following: the timing and completion of the stock split; our ability to sustain and/or surpass the current level of sales of our products, to adapt to changing consumer preferences, and to effectively respond to competitive products and pricing pressures; our ability to implement our growth strategy, including expanding our business in existing and new sectors and achieving profitability within our Alcohol Brands segment; our ability to adapt to the changing retail landscape with the rapid growth in e-commerce retailers and e-commerce websites; our ability to absorb, reduce or pass on to our bottlers/distributors increases in costs and expenses, including, but not limited to, increases to the cost of aluminum and other raw materials, the Midwest Premium, and freight costs; the impact of the current U.S. presidential administration’s policies on our energy drinks due to concerns about sugar-sweetened beverages, particular ingredients, such as food dyes, and the “generally recognized as safe” (GRAS) process; the impact of proposed or adopted domestic and/or foreign legislation to limit or restrict the sale of energy drinks (including the prohibition of the sale of energy drinks to certain demographics, at certain establishments, in certain container sizes or pursuant to certain governmental programs, such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)); the impact of changes in U.S. trade policies, including the imposition of additional tariffs; the impact of adverse changes in our costs, our supply chain, inflation or consumer demand for our products; the imposition of new and/or increased excise sales and/or other taxes on our products; our extensive commercial arrangements with The Coca-Cola Company (TCCC) and, as a result, our future performance’s substantial dependence on the success of our relationship with TCCC; the effects of unilateral decisions by bottlers/distributors and/or retailers on our business, including their distribution and placement of our products, their consolidation, their discontinuation, or restriction of the range of, all or any of our products that they carry, their limitations on the sale or sizes of our products, and/or their allocation of less resources to the sale of our products; changes in the price and/or availability of raw materials and other supply chain issues, such as the availability of products, suitable production facilities and/or co-packing arrangements; possible recalls of our products and/or the consequences and costs of defective production; disruption to our manufacturing facilities and operations related to climate, labor, production difficulties, capacity limitations, regulations or other causes; disruption to and/or lack of effectiveness of our information technology systems, including internal and external cybersecurity threats and breaches; adverse publicity surrounding obesity, alcohol consumption and other health concerns related to our products, product safety and quality; liabilities resulting from legal or regulatory proceedings, government investigations, and/or injunctions; the inherent operational risks, including the abuse or misuse of our products presented by the alcoholic beverage industry and/or related claims that may not be adequately covered by insurance or may lead to litigation; the current uncertainty and volatility in the national and global economy and changes in demand due to such economic conditions, including a slowdown in consumer spending generally; and the impact of military conflicts, including supply chain disruptions, volatility in commodity prices, increased economic uncertainty and escalating geopolitical tensions. For a more detailed discussion of these and other risks that could affect our operating results, see the Company’s reports filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including our annual report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025 and our subsequently filed quarterly report. The Company’s actual results could differ materially from those contained in the forward-looking statements. The Company assumes no obligation to update any forward-looking statements, whether as a result of new information, future events or otherwise.
